newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. urges India, Pakistan to launch peace talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges India, Pakistan to launch peace talks.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday urged Pakistan and India to start peace negotiations quickly and exhorted New Delhi as the larger, more powerful nation to show "accommodation" in bilateral talks.
U.S. ambassador to India Frank Wisner told a conference in Jammu and Kashmir state: "The time is ripe to resolve the conflict that has gripped this state for so long".
Spelling out U.S. policy towards India and Kashmir, Wisner said peace would not come to the region until the half-century-old dispute over the Himalayan region was resolved.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them sparked by tension over Kashmir.

Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah told the conference in the state's winter capital Jammu: "It is they (Pakistan) who invaded us twice in the past and sent their army earlier and killed and raped the people of the state."

More than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since a separatist revolt erupted in Jammu and Kashmir in 1990. India accuses Pakistan of arming guerrillas, but Islamabad says it provides only diplomatic support.
"We are capable of going into their territory and mopping them up but we never want that. We want friendship with them," Abdullah said.
Wisner said Washington did not seek to mediate over Kashmir.

"America's position regarding Jammu and Kashmir has remained constant over the years: the dispute needs to be resolved by India and Pakistan, taking into account the wishes of the people of the state," the U.S. envoy said.

Pakistan, citing a 1948 United Nations Security Council resolution, wants the people of mainly Moslem Kashmir to vote in an internationally supervised plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.
The two countries broke off talks in January 1994 after they bogged down in differences over Kashmir.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said last week that he favoured the resumption of talks, but would never relinquish the two-thirds of Kashmir controlled by India.
Pakistan's newly elected prime minister Nawaz Sharif said on Monday that he also wanted to revive talks, but New Delhi must be willing to let Kashmiris decide their own future.
Wisner said: "All the issues between India and Pakistan must be on the table for discussion, including Kashmir."

Wisner said India's new "Gujral Doctrine", named after Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, showed that India "as the larger, more powerful state in the region", was prepared to take the lead in being attentive to the needs of its neighbours.
"Peace with Pakistan should be pursued with dispatch, and in a spirit of accommodation," he said.
